title: Less urine, darker urine, and bladder or bowel changes

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no contributor interview, no claim of corpus completeness.
limitations: Public sources describe recognized patterns but do not supply firsthand room texture.
The record must not be used to diagnose, time, or manage a particular death.
Treatment, legal, ritual, and emergency decisions remain local and must be handled by qualified teams or relevant authorities.

moment.plain_scene: A dying person urinates less, the urine may look darker, bathroom trips become harder, or bladder and bowel control changes; witnesses may read the bed, pad, commode, catheter, or silence of no output as signs.

content_layers.observation_text: Public sources describe less urine, darker urine, and bladder/bowel changes as common near death; professional sources also treat markedly decreased urine output as a late sign while warning that signs are not perfect predictors.
content_layers.source_synthesis: NCI, NHS inform, Hospice UK, PCNOW, and healthdirect support a cautious record: changes in elimination are common, may require comfort and hygiene support, and must not be used as a stand-alone clock.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: This is one of the archive’s dignity records: what families remember may be the pad, the bed, the embarrassment, or the nurse who made the room ordinary again.

what_this_is_not: not a timing tool by itself
not a reason to shame the dying person
not a substitute for nursing advice on hygiene, skin, or comfort
uncertainties: Sources rarely preserve the emotional texture of embarrassment, cleaning, and family role changes.
Timing varies by illness, fluid intake, medications, and care setting.
The record needs care-aide and nursing testimony.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should normalize the possibility of bladder/bowel changes without making them sound trivial; it should route practical concerns to nurses or carers.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner surface should collect phrases and practices that protect dignity during cleaning, catheter discussions, and bed changes.
language_notes: Avoid euphemisms that hide what families actually need to search.
Pair “incontinence” with plain phrases like “losing control of bladder or bowels.”

provenance.provenance_statement: Drafted from named public sources to test the v2 witnessed-moment schema. It should be reviewed before any public surface uses it.

safety.clinical_boundary: This record is observational/source-indexing only. It is not medical advice, not a prognosis, and not a substitute for a local hospice, clinician, emergency, legal, cultural, or care team.
safety.safety_notes: Before public use, route through clinical safety review and ensure any lay surface directs urgent or worried readers to qualified local support.
